prompt: Per this module, what actually distinguishes 'taking ownership' of a feature from merging a single well-reviewed PR?
choices: Ownership requires the PR to touch more files than a typical contribution
Ownership means participating in the design discussion before coding, shipping the work across multiple related PRs, and handling follow-up maintenance after merge
Ownership is granted automatically once a contributor has ten merged PRs on a project
Ownership only requires writing more thorough tests than other contributors

prompt: In the pip-audit worked example, what was the actual bug in the version-range matcher?
choices: It crashed on any version string containing a pre-release suffix
It rejected all OSV advisories that used the ECOSYSTEM range type
It only evaluated the first introduced/fixed event pair, missing advisories with multiple disjoint (non-contiguous) vulnerable intervals
It compared versions as raw strings instead of using the packaging library at all

prompt: Why did the contributor propose a general 'sweep over all events' fix instead of just patching the matcher to read one more introduced/fixed pair?
choices: Because the sweep approach was shorter code to write
Because OSV's schema allows an arbitrary number of introduced/fixed pairs per range, so a pair-specific patch would just recur on the next multi-interval advisory
Because the maintainer refused to accept any PR under 50 lines
Because the project's style guide banned conditional branches in matcher functions

prompt: Why were the fix, the tests, and the docs/changelog update split into three separate PRs instead of one combined diff?
choices: The project's CI only allowed one file change per pull request
Splitting let each reviewable unit (behavior fix, proof via tests, and documentation for future contributors) be reviewed and landed independently
The maintainer required a minimum of three PRs per contributor each month
Tests and docs could not technically be included in the same repository as the fix

prompt: In the example maintainer-style review of the --ignore-vuln PR, which of the following best characterizes what made it a 'maintainer-track' review rather than a drive-by one?
choices: It approved the PR immediately with no comments, since the code compiled and tests passed
It only pointed out style nitpicks like variable naming and line length

It cited a concrete failure scenario with real inputs, explicitly declined to block on something that didn't matter while explaining why, asked a genuine open design question, and requested a test to pin down the answer either way
It rewrote the entire PR itself and pushed the changes directly to the contributor's branch without comment

prompt: Which signal most reliably distinguishes a 'recognized regular' from someone who merged one PR and vanished?
choices: Having a profile picture and bio filled out on their GitHub account
A maintainer referencing the contributor's past work from memory (e.g. 'isn't this the thing you fixed in #412?') or @-mentioning them for input on an unrelated issue in their area
The number of total lines of code changed across all their PRs combined
Whether they starred the repository before contributing

prompt: Why did the module treat the three-weeks-later regression fix (the pre-release version edge case) as an important part of 'ownership,' even though it was a small, one-line change?
choices: Because small fixes are inherently more impressive to maintainers than large ones
Because it demonstrates the contributor stayed accountable for the subsystem's correctness over time rather than disappearing once the original PRs merged
Because the fix required rewriting the entire matcher from scratch
Because the maintainer offered a monetary bounty for regression fixes
